The canonical non-implication concerns existing ordinary conditional means (standing_assumptions: each conditional mean is taken to exist). The existential stub, Defs/Part4.lean:115-119, has no integrability conditions and uses meanOn, Defs/Part3.lean:25-30, whose numerator is zero whenever the restricted integrand is not integrable. This can witness a wholly artificial inequality: let H be standard Cauchy, independent of fair Z, let Y0=H,Y1=H+1, and let both checks be always true and X=0. Both selected Bochner means are zero by totalization, whereas the integrable constant effect has mean one. Thus the stub's inequality 0!=1 need not involve existing selected means or selection at all, and does not certify the ordinary-mean claim. This is not vacuity or a claim that the literal Lean proposition is false; the bounded three-stratum example of T16 can satisfy a repaired statement.

The per-arm covariate ignorability assumption and common-check event match the claim, and covariateBalance is precisely conditional independence at each positive-probability Boolean check value, with the correctly normalized restricted measure. Arbitrary finite real covariate vectors and no positivity or integrability additions are used.

The canonical counterexample requires existing conditional means at a positive-mass covariate value. Fixing K=2, one constant covariate and value zero is a legitimate witness specialization, but dropping all three restricted-integrability conditions is not. Defs/Part4.lean:128-135 permits nonintegrable selected outcomes to have meanOn zero. The common-check Cauchy model described for T21, with X identically zero, satisfies all the written probability, ignorability, balance and positive-all-pass hypotheses and produces the totalized inequality 0!=1 although the selected ordinary means do not exist. Hence this is a different total-function assertion. A bounded genuine counterexample is available from T16.
